title: Design Principles (SOLID)
intro: What makes a design good or rotten, the goals of OO design (low coupling, high cohesion), and the five SOLID principles with a before/after picture for each. Expect questions that name a smell and ask which principle it breaks.

cards.title: Working is not the same as well designed
cards.body:
A program can run fine today and still be badly designed: it shows symptoms of breaking the moment you try to change it.

Good design is judged by how easily the software can be **changed, reused and maintained**, not only by whether it works now. The graph shows the idea: both designs work on day 1, but every change to a rotting design costs more than the last.

cards.title: Three symptoms of rotting design
cards.body:
The slides name three symptoms that a design is rotting:

**Rigidity**: hard to change, even in simple ways. Every change causes a cascade of changes in dependent modules (ripple/snowball effect).
**Fragility**: each change breaks the software in many places, often in areas with no conceptual link to the change.
**Immobility**: you can't reuse a module in another project (or another part of the same one) because of the baggage it depends on.

cards.title: OO design goals
cards.body:
Much of OO design is about **managing dependencies**. You can't write OO code without depending on something, so the aim is to keep a change in one class from forcing changes in others.

The slides' class design guidelines: manage coupling and cohesion, and design with **Reusability**, **Extensibility** and **Maintainability** in mind, to achieve **loose (low) coupling and high cohesion**.

cards.title: Coupling: tight vs loose
cards.body:
**Coupling** is how much one class depends on, or knows about, other classes.

**Tight**: classes need each other to work, so changing one forces changes in many (slides: NASDAQ checks DataDisplay's `displayType`).
**Loose (low)**: classes talk through small, well-defined interfaces. The slides' Bank Account fix puts `<<interface>>` Account and AccountInfoDisplay between Client and the concrete classes: "Interaction via interfaces promotes loose coupling."

Delegation ('has a') couples less than inheritance ('is a').

cards.title: Cohesion and encapsulation
cards.body:
**Cohesion** is how focused a class is. A highly cohesive class does one thing and does it well; a low-cohesion class is "not sure what it does" (the slides' one-man-with-every-tool picture).

Slides' Data Persistence example: `DataManager` validated customers by fetching and comparing passwords itself (bad encapsulation). The fix makes Customer and Account responsible for their own `validate()` and `store()`; DataManager just manages the entities.

cards.title: SOLID at a glance
cards.body:
The slides' five SOLID design principles. Each one is a different way to keep change local.

Note the slides call the D the **Dependency Injection Principle (DIP)**, also known as **Inversion of Control (IoC)**. Most textbooks call it the Dependency *Inversion* Principle; injection is the usual way to apply it. The rule is the same.

cards.title: S: Single Responsibility Principle
cards.body:
"There should never be more than ONE reason for a class to change."

Each responsibility is an **axis of change**. If a class has two responsibilities they become coupled: a change for one can break the other. Avoid the **god class**. The slides sum it up as **SRP = cohesion**.

**Smell:** you need "and" to describe the class, or different departments would ask for changes to it.

cards.title: O: Open-Closed Principle
cards.body:
"A module should be **open for extension** but **closed for modification**." (Bertrand Meyer)

You change what a module does by adding new code, without editing its source. **Abstraction is the key.** In the slides' fare example, a `switch (type)` inside Transport must be edited for every new transport. With an abstract Transport and one subclass per type, a Tricycle is just a new class.

**Smell:** a switch or if-else on a type code that grows with every new type.

cards.title: L: Liskov Substitution Principle
cards.body:
**Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.** Code written for the base class must still work when given any subclass (Barbara Liskov, 1988).

Classic example: Square extends Rectangle compiles, but each setter changes both sides, so a client that sets width 5 and height 10 gets 100, not 50. The fix: don't make Square a Rectangle; make both implement Shape.

**Smell:** an override that ignores, throws, or changes what the parent promised.

cards.after: **Design by contract:** a subclass method is substitutable if its **pre-conditions are no stronger** (expect no more) and its **post-conditions are no weaker** (provide no less). Slides' noodle analogy: the menu says $3 a bowl; a stall that demands $4 ("I need more!!") or gives half a bowl breaks the contract.
keypoints: Compiling is not enough: behaviour must stay correct.
Pre-conditions: no stronger. Post-conditions: no weaker.
Slides' ATMDisplay: expects non-null (more) and returns partial details (less) = 2 violations.

cards.title: I: Interface Segregation Principle
cards.body:
"Many client-specific interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface." Classes should not depend on interfaces they do not use. **Avoid FAT interfaces.**

Slides' example: IAnimal has fly(), run(), swim(), so Tiger has to write an empty `fly() { }`. Splitting it into IFlyable, IRunnable and ISwimmable lets each animal implement only what it can do. A Goose implements all three.

**Smell:** empty or dummy method bodies, or methods that throw "not supported".

cards.title: D: Dependency Injection Principle
cards.body:
A. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. **Both should depend on abstractions.**
B. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

Also called **Inversion of Control (IoC)**; it is at the heart of framework design. **Smell:** a high-level class does `new SomeConcreteClass()` inside itself, so you can't swap or test it without editing it.

cards.title: Which principle is it?
cards.body: When a question shows a design and asks which principle is violated, check the smells in this order. The first "yes" is usually the answer.
keypoints: God class → SRP. Switch on type → OCP.
Square/Ostrich, empty or throwing override → LSP.
Empty methods from a fat interface → ISP. `new Concrete()` in a high-level class → DIP.

keypoints: Mistake: "it compiles, so it's a valid subclass". LSP is about behaviour (Square compiles but breaks clients).
Mistake: thinking OCP means never touching code. It means adding new behaviour by **adding** classes.
Mistake: mixing up symptoms. Fragility = breaks in **unrelated** places; Rigidity = **cascade** of required changes; Immobility = can't **reuse**.
Mistake: more connections = better. Class design ≠ network design: aim for low coupling.
